title: Lucky accidents and missing names: how discoveries really happen

summary.text: Spencer Silver tried to make a very strong glue and made a weak one instead. Years later, his weak glue became the glue on sticky notes. Many discoveries began like this, with a result nobody wanted, and a person who stopped to ask why. You will make your own 'failed' tape and find a job it does better than good tape. You will also meet the people who did the work behind famous discoveries but were left out when the credit was handed out.
summary.art: A child's desk with a strip of tape that has torn a newspaper page, and beside it a small yellow paper note stuck lightly to a notebook, peeling off clean.

intro.hook: In 1968, a chemist named Spencer Silver tried to make a glue strong enough to help build aeroplanes. His glue came out so weak that paper stuck to it peeled straight off again. Was that a failure?
intro.text: For aeroplanes, yes. But six years later his co-worker Art Fry needed a bookmark that would stay in his song book without tearing the pages. Silver's weak glue was just right. A result is not good or bad by itself. It depends on what you need it for. In this unit you will test this with tape, and meet people whose 'mistakes' became discoveries.
intro.art: A man in a 1960s laboratory frowning at a strip of paper peeling off a glass plate, and a small inset of a song book with a yellow bookmark poking out.

outcomes: I can say what a discovery is, and how it is different from an invention.
I can tell the true story of a discovery that began with an accident or a mistake, and say what the person did that turned it into a discovery.
I can explain why an unexpected result must be checked and repeated before anyone can call it a discovery.
I can test a 'failed' material fairly, and use my results to say which job it does well.
I can name people who did important work on a discovery but were left out of the credit, and give reasons why this happens.
I can argue for one side of a question about credit, use evidence, and say what the other side has right.

terms.meaning: Finding out something true about the world that people did not know before, and showing others that it is true.
terms.example: Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered pulsars, stars that send out radio pulses as regular as a clock.
terms.art: A girl with a torch finding a glowing shell under a dark shelf, her face lit with surprise.

terms.meaning: Something new that a person makes or designs, such as a tool, a machine or a material.
terms.example: The sticky note is an invention. Finding out how glue grips paper is a discovery.
terms.art: Two boxes side by side: one labelled 'found' with a magnifying glass over a leaf, one labelled 'made' with a hand building a paper boat.

terms.meaning: Something that happens without anyone planning it.
terms.example: Alexander Fleming did not plan for mould to land on his dish of bacteria. It was an accident.
terms.art: A glass dish with a fuzzy green spot of mould on one side and a clear ring around the mould.

terms.meaning: Something done wrongly, or a result that is not what you were trying to get.
terms.example: William Perkin was trying to make a medicine for malaria. His mistake made a bright purple dye instead.
terms.art: A teenage boy in an old-fashioned home laboratory holding up a flask of bright purple liquid.

terms.meaning: Finding something good that you were not looking for, by luck and by noticing. The word comes from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka.
terms.example: Finding a forgotten 100-rupee note in an old school bag is a small piece of serendipity.
terms.art: A map of Sri Lanka marked 'Serendip' in old letters, with three princes on horseback looking at tracks on the ground.

terms.meaning: Looking at something carefully, with any of your senses, and noting what you see.
terms.example: Jocelyn Bell Burnell's observation was a tiny wobble on a long paper chart, a mark most people would have missed.
terms.art: A young woman bent over a long paper chart with a pencil, circling a tiny wobble in the line.

terms.meaning: What actually happens in a test or an experiment.
terms.example: In the tape test, one result was that fresh tape tore the newspaper.
terms.art: A strip of tape lifted off a newspaper page, carrying a torn grey patch of paper with it.

terms.meaning: What you saw or measured that shows whether an idea is true.
terms.example: The mice that got penicillin lived and the mice that did not get it died. That was evidence that penicillin worked inside a body.
terms.art: Two small cages of white mice side by side, one with four lively mice and one empty, with a notebook between them.

terms.meaning: Any material that sticks things together, such as glue, gum or the sticky layer on tape.
terms.example: The sticky layer on a bindi is an adhesive. So is the rice paste some families use to close envelopes.
terms.art: A tube of glue, a roll of tape, a bindi on a card and a small bowl of rice paste.

terms.meaning: A very thin thread. Paper is made of tiny plant fibres pressed into a flat mat.
terms.example: Tear a newspaper slowly and look at the edge. You can see the furry fibres sticking out.
terms.art: A close-up of a torn paper edge, with tiny fibres sticking out like the end of a frayed rope.

terms.meaning: Saying, out loud or in writing, who did a piece of work, so that people know and thank them.
terms.example: At the end of a film, the credits list everyone who made it, from the actors to the cooks.
terms.art: A film screen scrolling a long list of names on a dark background.

terms.meaning: A student at a university who does real scientific research under a teacher, called a supervisor, to earn a degree.
terms.example: Jocelyn Bell Burnell was a research student when she found the first pulsar. Antony Hewish was her supervisor.
terms.art: A young woman and an older man standing in a field of wooden poles and wires, a radio telescope.

terms.meaning: A famous prize given each year for great work in physics, chemistry, medicine, writing and peace. At most three people can share one prize.
terms.example: C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for the Raman effect.
terms.art: A round gold medal with a man's face on it, lying on a velvet cloth.

terms.meaning: A fungus that grows as soft, fuzzy patches on old food and damp walls.
terms.example: Bread left in a damp box for a week grows green or black mould.
terms.art: A slice of bread with fuzzy green and white patches of mould, shown under a magnifying glass.

terms.meaning: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing inside the body. Penicillin was the first one used widely.
terms.example: A doctor may give an antibiotic for a bad throat infection caused by bacteria.
terms.art: A strip of medicine tablets next to a drawing of round bacteria with a cross over them.

terms.meaning: A dead star, smaller than a city, that spins very fast and sends out a beam of radio waves that sweeps past the Earth like a lighthouse.
terms.example: The first pulsar sends a radio pulse to Earth about every one and a third seconds.
terms.art: A small bright ball in space with two beams coming out of its top and bottom, sweeping past a tiny Earth.

explanations.definition: A discovery is finding out something true about the world that people did not know before, and showing others that it is true. An invention is something new that a person makes.
explanations.description: Pulsars spun in space for millions of years before anyone knew about them. Jocelyn Bell Burnell did not make them. She found them, so that is a discovery. A sticky note did not exist until people made it, so that is an invention. The two often go together. Finding out how a weak glue behaves is a discovery. Turning it into sticky notes is an invention. A discovery also needs other people to check it. If only one person has seen something and nobody else can see it again, it is not yet a discovery.
examples: Finding that the mould Penicillium makes a substance that kills bacteria was a discovery. Making penicillin into a medicine in bottles was an invention.
C. V. Raman discovered that light changes colour very slightly when it bounces off molecules. Nobody invented that. It was always happening.
explanations.art: A split picture: on one side a girl finding a shell on a beach, on the other a girl building a toy boat from paper.
explanations.context: This card says what a discovery is, and how it is different from an invention.

explanations.concept: Accidents and mistakes that became discoveries
explanations.definition: Many discoveries began with something nobody planned, or with an experiment that went wrong. The accident gave a surprising result. A person then noticed it and asked why.
explanations.description: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming came back from a holiday to his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London. On one glass dish of bacteria, a mould had grown by accident. Around the mould was a clear ring where the bacteria had died. Fleming named the substance from the mould penicillin. In 1856, William Perkin, aged 18, tried to make quinine, a medicine for malaria, in a laboratory at his home in London. He got a dark sludge. When he cleaned it out with alcohol, it turned a bright purple. That was mauve, the first dye made from chemicals rather than plants or insects. In 1896, Henri Becquerel in Paris planned to put uranium salts in sunlight, but the sky stayed cloudy. He left them in a drawer on top of a wrapped photographic plate, and developed the plate anyway. It was fogged. The uranium was giving out rays all by itself, with no sunlight at all. Marie Curie later named this radioactivity.
examples: Fleming's dish of bacteria was 'spoilt' by mould. The spoilt dish led to penicillin.
Perkin failed to make quinine and made the first chemical dye instead. Mauve soon became a very popular colour for clothes.
Spencer Silver's glue was too weak for aeroplanes. It became the glue on sticky notes.
explanations.art: Three small scenes in a row: a glass dish with mould and a clear ring, a flask of purple liquid, and a photographic plate with a dark blurry shape on it.
explanations.context: This card tells three true stories in which an accident or a mistake led to a discovery.

explanations.concept: Why only some people notice: the prepared mind
explanations.description: Mould must have landed on other people's dishes before 1928. Most of them threw the dish away. In 1854, the French scientist Louis Pasteur said, 'In the fields of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind.' He meant that luck helps only people who already know enough to see that something is strange. Fleming had studied bacteria-killing substances for years, so a clear ring meant something to him. Bell Burnell knew exactly what her chart should look like, so she noticed a mark that did not belong. This is an idea about how people think, not a law of nature. Some discoveries were made by beginners who looked with fresh eyes.
examples: A cook who has made dosa batter a hundred times notices at once when it smells different. A new cook may not.
Bell Burnell checked many metres of paper chart by hand every week. She knew its usual wiggles so well that a tiny strange mark stood out.
explanations.art: A girl looking closely at a row of identical idlis and pointing at the one with a different shape.
explanations.context: Accidents happen to everyone. This card is about why some people notice an accident and make it a discovery, and others do not.

explanations.concept: A surprise is only the start
explanations.definition: An unexpected result becomes a discovery only after it has been checked, repeated and explained. Most surprising results turn out to be errors.
explanations.description: When something odd happens, the first question is: did I make a mistake? Bell Burnell's strange mark could have been a fault in the machine, or a signal from a car or a radio on Earth. She and her supervisor checked. The mark came back about four minutes earlier each day, the same way the stars do. Signals from Earth do not do that. So it came from out in space. Fleming grew the mould again in fresh dishes, and the bacteria died again. Penicillin worked in a dish. It still had to be shown to work inside a living body. In May 1940, at Oxford, Howard Florey's team gave eight mice a deadly infection. Four mice also got penicillin. By the next morning the four without penicillin had died. The four with penicillin were alive.
examples: Bell Burnell checked whether the signal kept time with the stars. It did, so it was not coming from Earth.
The Oxford team compared mice with penicillin and mice without it. This is a fair test, like the ones you have done.
explanations.art: A notebook page with a table: 'Day, time the mark appeared', the times getting four minutes earlier each day, and a small sketch of stars.
explanations.context: This card says what scientists do after a surprising result, before they call it a discovery.

explanations.concept: Why strong tape tears paper and weak tape does not
explanations.definition: Tape sticks because its glue presses very close to the surface and grips it. If the glue grips the paper's fibres harder than the fibres grip each other, the paper tears when you peel the tape.
explanations.description: Paper is a mat of tiny plant fibres pressed together. Fresh cello tape has a smooth, even layer of glue. It touches the paper almost everywhere and grips the fibres tightly. When you peel it, the top fibres hold on to the glue and leave the rest of the paper behind. That is the grey, furry patch you saw. When you dab tape on a cloth, tiny cotton fibres stick to the glue and cover parts of it. Less glue can touch the paper, so it grips more gently. It can come off without tearing anything. Spencer Silver's glue worked in a similar way. It was made of tiny balls of sticky material. The balls touched the paper only at some points, so the glue held lightly and let go cleanly.
examples: Fresh cello tape on a newspaper usually tears the paper when you peel it.
A sticky note can be stuck and moved many times, because its glue touches the page only in some places.
A bindi can be peeled off the forehead and stuck again, because its glue is a gentle one.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drawing: above, smooth glue pressing on every paper fibre; below, small glue balls touching the fibres only at a few points.
explanations.context: Remember the Too-Weak Tape Test, where some tape tore the newspaper and some came off clean? This card explains why.

explanations.concept: How credit is given in science
explanations.definition: Scientists get credit when their names are on the report of the work, called a paper, when a discovery is named after them, and when they win prizes.
explanations.description: When scientists find something, they write it up in a paper and send it to a science journal. The names of the people who did the work go at the top. These people are the authors. The first name is often the person who did the most, but different fields use different rules. Sometimes a discovery is named after one person, such as the Raman effect. Big prizes add even more credit. A Nobel Prize can be shared by at most three people. Today many discoveries are made by large teams. The 2016 paper that announced the first gravitational waves, ripples in space, had more than a thousand authors. No prize can name them all.
examples: The 1968 paper announcing pulsars had five authors. Antony Hewish was first and Jocelyn Bell was second.
In 1928, C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan wrote the paper about the new kind of light scattering together. It came to be called the Raman effect.
explanations.art: A printed science paper with a title and five names at the top, and a magnifying glass over the second name.
explanations.context: This card explains how scientists get credit for a discovery: names on papers, names on discoveries, and prizes.

explanations.concept: Who gets left out, and why
explanations.description: Many people who did important work were left out of the credit. Norman Heatley worked out how to grow and clean enough penicillin for the Oxford tests. The 1945 Nobel Prize went to Fleming, Florey and Chain. Heatley was not named, and his work was honoured properly only in 1990. Rosalind Franklin took the X-ray photograph that showed the shape of DNA. Her co-worker Maurice Wilkins showed it to James Watson without asking her. Watson, Francis Crick and Wilkins won the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize is not given after death. People argue about why this happens so often. Common reasons are that the person was young, a woman, an assistant, or worked far from famous universities.
examples: Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first pulsar as a research student. The 1974 Nobel Prize went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and to Martin Ryle.
K. S. Krishnan did the Raman effect experiments with C. V. Raman. Only Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize.

perspectives.who: Fred Hoyle, a famous astronomer, at the time
perspectives.explanation: Hoyle said that Bell Burnell's discovery was the key step, and that the prize should have included her.

She said that a supervisor is responsible for a project's success or failure, and that Nobel Prizes should not usually go to research students. Much later she also said that being a student and a woman lowered her standing.

perspectives.who: People who defend the prize rules
perspectives.explanation: They say that the person who designed the project and built the telescope deserves the credit, and that a prize must draw a line somewhere.

explanations.art: A long table of scientists in white coats, with three of them lit up by a spotlight and the rest in shadow.
explanations.context: This card is about people who did important work on a discovery but were left out of the credit, and why people still argue about it.

explanations.definition: Two scientists from South India did key work on famous discoveries, and are much less well known than their partners.
explanations.description: K. S. Krishnan was born in 1898 near Watrap, in what is now Virudhunagar district of Tamil Nadu. In Kolkata, he worked with C. V. Raman on how light scatters, or bounces off, the tiny particles of liquids. In 1928 they found that a little of the scattered light comes back with a changed colour. They wrote the paper together. The discovery was named after Raman, and only Raman won the Nobel Prize in 1930. Yellapragada Subbarow was born in 1895 in Bhimavaram, in Andhra Pradesh. In the 1920s at Harvard University in the USA, he and Cyrus Fiske found two substances that muscles use for energy: phosphocreatine and ATP. Later his team made folic acid, a vitamin, in the laboratory, and early medicines for cancer. Harvard never made him a permanent professor, and few people today know his name.
examples: India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February, the day in 1928 when the Raman effect was announced.
ATP is the energy carrier in every cell of your body. Subbarow was one of the first to find out what it does in muscles.
explanations.art: Two portraits side by side in pencil: a young Indian man with round glasses beside a light beam through a flask, and a man in a 1940s laboratory with test tubes.
explanations.context: This card tells two true stories of scientists from South India whose work was less credited than their partners'.

explanations.description: When a discovery story is told again and again, it often shrinks to one person and one magic moment. Fleming's mould is usually told without the Oxford team who turned it into a medicine. The story that Archimedes jumped out of his bath shouting 'Eureka!' was first written down about 200 years after he died. Nobody knows if it happened. There is also a popular story that a laboratory worker named Mary Hunt found a mouldy melon in a market in Peoria, USA, in 1943, and that its mould made far more penicillin than Fleming's. The melon mould was real and did make far more. Whether Mary Hunt was the one who found it is not certain. Short stories are easy to remember. Real discoveries usually take many people and many years.
examples: Fleming saw the clear ring in 1928. Penicillin was first given to patients in 1941. That took 13 years and many people.
The best penicillin mould came from a melon sold in a market in Peoria, USA, in 1943.
explanations.art: A storybook open on a lap, showing one man and a light bulb, with a crowd of faint people standing behind him on the page.
explanations.context: This card is about how true discovery stories get shortened over time, until only one name is left.

explanations.concept: Does hot water freeze faster than cold water?
explanations.description: In 1963, Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy in Tanzania, was making ice cream at school. There was not much space in the freezer, so he put his hot milk mixture in without waiting for it to cool. It froze before his friends' cooler mixtures. His teacher told him he must be confused. Later, a visiting physics professor, Denis Osborne, tried it in his own laboratory and got the same result. In 1969 the two of them wrote a paper together, and the idea is now called the Mpemba effect. But many careful tests since then have not found it. It seems to depend on the container, the freezer and how you decide when water has 'frozen'. Scientists still argue about whether it is real.
examples: Mpemba was laughed at for saying hot milk froze first. He kept asking until a scientist tested it.
In some home tests the hot water freezes first, and in others the cold water does. Try it and see what yours does.

perspectives.who: Scientists who have seen the effect
perspectives.explanation: Hot water loses some water as steam, so there is less left to freeze. Hot water may also set up stronger currents inside the cup that carry heat away faster.
In tests where everything is kept exactly the same, cold water almost always freezes first. They think the effect comes from small differences that are hard to control, such as frost under one cup.

explanations.art: A boy in a school uniform in the 1960s opening a small freezer, holding a cup of ice cream mixture, with a teacher frowning behind him.
explanations.context: This card tells the true story of Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy whose surprising result was laughed at, and is still argued about today.

agreed.text: Many important discoveries began with an accident or an unexpected result.
agreed.evidence: The stories of penicillin (1928), mauve dye (1856), radioactivity (1896) and pulsars (1967) were written down at the time by the people involved.

agreed.text: An unexpected result must be checked and repeated before it counts as a discovery.
agreed.evidence: Fleming grew the mould again, Bell Burnell checked that the signal kept time with the stars, and the Oxford team tested penicillin on mice before giving it to people.

agreed.text: Most discoveries need many people, not one.
agreed.evidence: Penicillin needed Fleming, Florey, Chain, Heatley, Dorothy Hodgkin who worked out its shape in 1945, and many factory workers. Science papers today often have dozens or even thousands of authors.

agreed.text: Some people who did key work were left out of prizes and famous stories.
agreed.evidence: Norman Heatley, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Rosalind Franklin and K. S. Krishnan were not included in Nobel Prizes for discoveries they worked on. The records of the prizes and papers show who did what.

agreed.text: Paper tears when a glue grips its fibres harder than the fibres grip each other.
agreed.evidence: You can see torn fibres stuck to the peeled tape with a magnifying glass. Scientists who study adhesives measure how hard glue grips with special machines.

challenging.claim: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin all by himself, and that is why we have the medicine.
challenging.who: A very common way the story is told
challenging.for: Fleming really did notice the mould, name penicillin and write the first paper about it in 1929.
challenging.against: Fleming could not make enough pure penicillin to treat anyone. Florey, Chain, Heatley and their Oxford team did that from 1939 to 1941. American laboratories then found ways to make it in huge amounts.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story that leaves most of the people out.

challenging.claim: Most great discoveries are lucky accidents.
challenging.who: A popular idea, because accident stories are the ones people remember
challenging.for: Penicillin, mauve, radioactivity, X-rays and pulsars all began with something unexpected.
challenging.against: Most discoveries come from long, planned work. Even the lucky ones needed years of knowledge to be noticed, and years of checking afterwards.
challenging.context: This card asks whether luck is really the main way discoveries are made.

challenging.claim: Jocelyn Bell Burnell should have shared the 1974 Nobel Prize.
challenging.who: Fred Hoyle and many astronomers since
challenging.for: She built part of the telescope, found the signal, and insisted it was real when others thought it was a fault.
challenging.against: Her supervisor designed the project and the telescope, and she herself said in 1977 that the prize should not usually go to research students.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument over who should have got the credit for discovering pulsars.

challenging.claim: Hot water freezes faster than cold water.
challenging.who: Erasto Mpemba and Denis Osborne (1969), and some later scientists
challenging.for: Mpemba saw it with ice cream, and Osborne saw it again in his laboratory.
challenging.against: Many careful tests since then find that cold water freezes first when everything else is kept the same.
challenging.context: This card is about the Mpemba effect, which scientists still argue about.

challenging.claim: A failed experiment is wasted time.
challenging.who: A common feeling when a test does not work
challenging.for: A failed experiment does not answer the question you asked, and it costs time and materials.
challenging.against: A failure tells you what does not work, and sometimes gives a result that is useful for a different question, like Silver's weak glue.
challenging.context: This card asks whether an experiment that fails is ever useful.

big_questions.q: Penicillium mould was killing bacteria long before any person noticed. Was penicillin discovered in 1928, or only noticed?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between a thing being there and a person knowing it is there.

big_questions.q: Your weak tape was a failure for one job and a success for another. Is anything a failure for every job?
big_questions.hint: Think of a broken pencil, a torn sheet of paper, or a burnt chapati. Can you find a use for each?

big_questions.q: If a whole team makes a discovery, should a prize ever go to just one person?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cricket team. Who gets the 'player of the match' award, and is that fair to the others?

big_questions.q: Bell Burnell's chart showed the pulsar in August 1967, but she found the mark only in November. How many discoveries might be sitting in old notebooks right now, not yet noticed?
big_questions.hint: Scientists today find new things in old photographs of the sky taken a hundred years ago.

big_questions.q: Why do we remember one name for a discovery, even when many people did the work?
big_questions.hint: Think about how a story changes when it is told many times. What is easy to remember?

big_questions.q: Mpemba's teacher said he was confused. When should you trust your own eyes over a teacher or a book?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would make you sure: seeing it once, or seeing it again in a fair test?

story.title: The Curd on Top of the Fridge
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: milk sets into curd faster when it is kept warm, and the top of many fridges is warm, because a fridge pushes heat out at the back and warm air rises.
text: Divya was ten and lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Chennai. Her school science fair was on Monday. Her question was written at the top of a big chart paper: 'Where in our flat does curd set best?'
On Saturday evening, Amma warmed a pan of milk until it felt just warm on Divya's wrist. Divya poured it into three small steel bowls. Into each bowl she stirred one spoon of yesterday's curd.
She put one bowl on the kitchen shelf. She put one on the balcony, in the shade. She put the third bowl inside the fridge. Then she wrote the time on her chart: 7 o'clock.
Her brother Arjun was seven. He wanted a bowl too. So Divya filled a fourth bowl for him, the same way.
"Where shall I keep mine?" he asked.
"Anywhere," said Divya. She was busy drawing her table.
Arjun looked around. Their cat, Mittai, loved milk. Arjun climbed on a stool and pushed his bowl right to the back of the top of the fridge, where Mittai could not reach. Then he forgot all about it.
On Sunday morning, Divya checked her three bowls. She tipped each one a little, carefully.
The bowl from the fridge was still milk. It sloshed. The bowl from the balcony was thick at the bottom but runny on top. The bowl from the kitchen shelf was soft curd that wobbled.
"The kitchen shelf wins," said Divya, and began to write it down.
Then Arjun remembered. He climbed up on the stool and brought down his bowl. He tipped it right over. Nothing moved. The curd was firm and thick. It was the best curd of all.
Divya stared at it. "Where was that?"
"On top of the fridge," said Arjun. "To keep it from Mittai."
"But the top of the fridge isn't in my test," said Divya. She felt cross. Her chart was nearly finished. Now this bowl did not fit.
Selvi akka, who came every morning to help Amma cook, was rolling out chapatis. She laughed. "Put your hand up there," she said.
Divya climbed onto the stool and put her hand on top of the fridge. It was warm, like a sunny wall.

"A fridge is cold inside," said Selvi akka, "but it pushes the heat out at the back. Warm air rises, so the top gets warm. In my village, my mother kept the curd pot near the stove, where the ashes stayed warm all night. Curd likes to be kept warm."
"So that's why the fridge bowl never set," said Divya slowly. "It was too cold. And the balcony was cooler than the shelf in the night."
Arjun grinned. "So I won."
"You didn't plan it," said Divya. "It was an accident."
"It was still the best curd," said Arjun.
Divya thought about that. Arjun's bowl had not been part of her plan. But it was the most interesting result she had. If she left it out, her chart would be tidier. It would also be less true.
"We have to check it," she said. "One bowl could be a fluke."

So on Sunday evening they did it all again, with four bowls this time. Divya put the fourth bowl on top of the fridge on purpose. On Monday morning, before school, she tipped them one by one. The top of the fridge won again.
At the science fair, her teacher, Mrs Rao, read the chart carefully. "This is a very good discovery, Divya," she said. "Well done."
Divya pointed to the bottom of the chart. She had added a box there, in her neatest writing. It said: 'Found by accident by Arjun Kumar, aged 7. Explained by Selvi akka. Checked again by Divya.'
Mrs Rao smiled. "Most discoveries should have a box like that," she said. "Very few of them do."
That evening, Arjun asked if they could test the top of the television next.
story.epiphany: For the parent: milk sets into curd because bacteria from the spoon of old curd grow in the milk and turn its sugar into an acid, which thickens it. They work fastest when it is warm, and very slowly in the cold. The top of a fridge is often warm because the fridge pushes heat out through the coils at the back, and warm air rises. Divya's planned test missed the best place. Arjun's accident found it, Selvi akka explained it, and Divya checked it by repeating the test. A discovery usually needs all three: a surprise, an explanation and a check. Divya's box at the bottom of the chart gives credit to all three people.
ask: Why did the curd inside the fridge not set?
Arjun did not plan his result. Why did Divya still include it?
Why did Divya test the top of the fridge a second time?
Who do you think should get the most credit for the discovery: Arjun, Selvi akka or Divya? Why?
Mrs Rao said that very few discoveries have a box like Divya's. Why do you think that is?

games.context: This is a card game about how discoveries really started. You sort true discovery stories into accidents, mistakes and careful plans, and win points for saying who did the work.

printables.title: 16 discovery cards
items: 1928, London. Mould lands on Alexander Fleming's dish of bacteria while he is on holiday. The bacteria near the mould die. (Accident)
1856, London. William Perkin, aged 18, tries to make the malaria medicine quinine and gets a bright purple dye. (Mistake)
1896, Paris. Henri Becquerel waits for sun, but it is cloudy. He leaves uranium on a wrapped photo plate in a drawer, and it fogs the plate. (Accident)
1968, USA. Spencer Silver tries to make a super-strong glue and makes a very weak one. (Mistake)
1967, Cambridge. Jocelyn Bell checks every metre of her telescope chart and finds a tiny regular mark. (Plan: careful checking)
1747, at sea. James Lind gives six pairs of sick sailors six different treatments to find which cures scurvy. (Plan)
1940, Oxford. Howard Florey's team gives penicillin to four sick mice and none to four others. (Plan)
1963, Tanzania. Erasto Mpemba puts his ice cream mixture in the freezer while it is still hot, because there is no time to cool it. (Accident)
1895, Germany. Wilhelm Röntgen sees a screen across his lab glowing while his tube is covered in black card. (Accident)
1928, Kolkata. C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan shine light through liquids for months to look for a tiny change in colour. (Plan)
1945, Oxford. Dorothy Hodgkin uses X-rays to work out the shape of penicillin. (Plan)
1943, Peoria, USA. A mouldy melon from a market grows a mould that makes far more penicillin. (Accident)
1929, Harvard, USA. Yellapragada Subbarow and Cyrus Fiske measure what muscles use for energy and find ATP. (Plan)
1952, London. Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling take an X-ray photo that shows the shape of DNA. (Plan)
1974, USA. Art Fry wants a bookmark that won't fall out of his song book, and remembers Silver's weak glue. (Plan using an old mistake)
Your own card: the tape you dabbed on cloth turned out best for moving a note. (Mistake on purpose)

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Named who did the work (1 point)
Named someone left out (1 bonus point)

setup.art: Three cards in a row on a table labelled ACCIDENT, MISTAKE and PLAN, with a face-down pile of discovery cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three sorting cards and the pile of discovery cards.

setup.art: A child placing a card about a mouldy dish under the ACCIDENT card while a parent writes on a score sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, sort it, and name who did the work.

rules: Lay the three sorting cards in a row: ACCIDENT, MISTAKE, PLAN.
Shuffle the discovery cards and put them face down. Cover the answer in brackets with your thumb when you read.
On your turn, read the top card out loud and put it under ACCIDENT, MISTAKE or PLAN.
Check the answer in brackets. A right sort scores 1 point.
Then name one person who did the work. That scores 1 more point.
If you can name someone who was left out of the credit for that discovery, score a bonus point.
Playing alone? Sort all 16 cards, then check your answers and add up your score.
When all the cards are played, the highest score wins.

flow.do: Lay out the three sorting cards and shuffle the discovery cards.
flow.say: Some discoveries begin with an accident, some with a mistake, and some with a careful plan. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Put out the three cards: Accident, Mistake, Plan. Mix up the discovery cards. You will sort them.
flow.context: This is the start of Accident, Mistake or Plan? You sort true discovery stories by how they began.

flow.do: Play the Spencer Silver card together as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Spencer Silver tries to make a strong glue and makes a weak one. Accident, mistake or plan?
flow.kid: Practice card. Spencer Silver wants strong glue and makes weak glue. Accident, mistake or plan?

check.q: Spencer Silver tried to make a strong glue and made a weak one. Which pile does this card go in?
check.why: Silver did the work on purpose, but the result was not what he was trying to get. That makes it a mistake. An accident is something nobody planned at all, like mould falling onto Fleming's dish.

flow.do: Take turns reading, sorting and naming people. Keep score.
flow.say: Read your card, sort it, then name who did the work. Can anyone name someone who was left out?
flow.kid: Read your card. Put it in a pile. Name who did the work. Know someone who was left out? Bonus point!
flow.parent: Some cards are arguable. Art Fry used an old mistake on purpose. Bell Burnell's find was lucky, but she found it by careful checking. If your child argues for a different pile with a good reason, give the point.

flow.do: Count the cards in each pile.
flow.say: Look at the three piles. Were there more accidents, mistakes or plans? Did even the accidents need careful work afterwards?
flow.kid: Count each pile. Which pile is biggest? Did the accidents need careful work too?

ask.q: Did any accident become a discovery without careful work afterwards?
good: No. Each one had to be checked and tested.
Fleming had to grow the mould again, and the Oxford team had to test penicillin.

games.title: Build the Team
games.context: This is a card game about how a discovery needs a whole team. You collect job cards to build a team that can make a discovery, then decide who gets the prize.

printables.title: 24 job cards (4 of each job)
items: NOTICER: spots the strange result. (4 cards)
CHECKER: repeats the test to make sure it is real. (4 cards)
EXPLAINER: works out why it happens. (4 cards)
MAKER: builds the machine or makes enough of the stuff. (4 cards)
WRITER: writes the paper so everyone can know. (4 cards)
LEADER: plans the project and finds the money. (4 cards)

printables.title: 4 PRIZE cards
items: PRIZE: name up to 3 people from your team.
PRIZE: name up to 3 people from your team.
PRIZE: name up to 3 people from your team.
PRIZE: name up to 3 people from your team.

printables.title: Name tokens: small paper slips to write a made-up team member's name on

setup.art: Job cards fanned out in two players' hands, labelled Noticer, Checker, Explainer, Maker, Writer and Leader, with a pile in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Deal 3 job cards each. Collect all six jobs.

setup.art: A child laying down six job cards with a name slip on each, and holding a PRIZE card, looking thoughtful.
setup.caption: 2. Name your team, then choose only three for the prize.

rules: Shuffle the job cards. Deal 3 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, take one card from the pile. Then put one card you don't need face up beside the pile.
You may take the top face-up card instead of one from the pile.
When you hold all six jobs, put them down and shout 'Discovery!' You have made a discovery.
Give each job card a name token, so your team has six people.
Now take a PRIZE card. You may name only 3 of your 6 people for the prize. Say who, and why.
Every other player gives you 1 point if they agree your choice was fair, or you may refuse the prize and name all six instead.

flow.do: Deal 3 job cards to each player and read out the six jobs.
flow.say: A discovery needs six jobs: noticer, checker, explainer, maker, writer and leader. Collect all six to make a discovery.
flow.kid: Read the six jobs. Noticer, checker, explainer, maker, writer, leader. Collect all six to make a discovery!
flow.context: This is the start of Build the Team. You collect the six jobs a discovery needs.

flow.do: Play until someone has all six jobs.
flow.say: Take a card, put one down. Which job are you still missing?
flow.kid: Take a card. Put one down. Which job do you still need?

check.q: In the pulsar story, which job did Jocelyn Bell do first?
check.why: Bell noticed the strange mark on the chart, so she was the noticer. She was also a checker and helped build the telescope, so she was a maker too. Her supervisor Antony Hewish was the leader.

flow.do: The winner names their team, then picks only three for the prize. Everyone talks about whether it is fair.
flow.say: You may name only three people for the prize. Who do you leave out? How do you think they will feel?
flow.kid: Name your six team members. Now pick only three for the prize. Who do you leave out? Is that fair?
flow.parent: There is no right answer. Listen for reasons: 'The noticer, because without her there is no discovery,' or 'The leader, because she planned it all.' Some children refuse the prize, which is a fine answer too.
flow.think: Is there a fairer prize than one that names only three people?

experiments.title: The Too-Weak Tape Test
experiments.context: In this experiment you make tape weaker on purpose, the way Spencer Silver's glue came out weak by mistake. Then you find out which tape is best for which job.
experiments.question: If we make tape weaker by dabbing it on cloth, is it worse at every job, or better at some?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will test four strips of tape: one fresh, and three dabbed on a cloth 3, 8 and 15 times. Which strip will hold a paper note best? Which one will come off the newspaper without tearing it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four strips come from the same roll, are cut the same length, and go on the same newspaper page. Each is pressed down the same way, with one thumb rub, and peeled the same way, slowly. Only the number of dabs on the cloth is different.
results_table: Did the note stay on when shaken? (yes or no)
Did the newspaper tear when you peeled it? (yes, a little, or no)
How many times did it stick again? (0 to 5)

materials.item: a roll of clear cello tape, the ordinary kind
a clean cotton cloth: an old cotton shirt, a hand towel or a cotton dupatta
a full page of plain newspaper, not the shiny magazine pages
4 small paper notes, each about 5 cm square, cut from an old notebook
a pencil, a ruler and scissors

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Nothing else in this test is dangerous.

schedule.what: Make four tape strips, dab three of them on a cloth, then test each one for holding, tearing and sticking again.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then circle the best strip for a note you want to move around, and the best strip for a note that must never fall off.

setup.art: Four strips of clear tape stuck by one end to the edge of a table, labelled A, B, C and D on small paper flags, with a cotton cloth beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut four strips of tape. Label them A, B, C and D.

setup.art: A child's hand pressing a strip of tape onto a folded cotton cloth and lifting it off, with tiny fibres on the sticky side.
setup.caption: 2. Dab B, C and D on a cloth: 3, 8 and 15 times.

setup.art: Four small paper notes taped across the top onto a newspaper page, each with its letter written on it.
setup.caption: 3. Tape a paper note onto the newspaper with each strip.

setup.art: A child peeling a strip of tape off a newspaper page, the strip carrying a grey torn patch of paper.
setup.caption: 4. Shake the page, then peel each strip slowly. Did the paper tear?

flow.do: 1. Show your child a strip of tape. 2. Tell them the true story of Spencer Silver's weak glue in two sentences.
flow.say: In 1968, Spencer Silver tried to make a very strong glue. It came out so weak that paper peeled off it easily. Today we will make our own weak tape and test it.
flow.kid: In 1968, Spencer Silver wanted a very strong glue. His glue came out weak. Paper peeled off it easily. Today you will make weak tape too. Then you will test it.
flow.parent: You only need the outline of the story here. The full story comes later, after the test, so the result is still a surprise.
flow.context: This is the start of the Too-Weak Tape Test. You hear why someone might want a weak glue at all.

flow.do: 1. Cut four strips of tape, each 6 cm long. 2. Fold over 1 cm at one end of each, sticky side to sticky side, to make a handle. 3. Write A, B, C and D on the handles. 4. Stick each one lightly by its far end to the table edge.
flow.say: A folded end gives you a handle. Then the glue on your fingers won't change the test.
flow.kid: Cut four strips of tape. Each one is 6 cm long. Fold over one end to make a handle. Write A, B, C and D on the handles.
flow.parent: Help with the scissors and the measuring. Keep the strips the same length, because a longer strip has more glue and would hold better anyway.

flow.do: 1. Leave strip A as it is. 2. Press strip B onto the cotton cloth and lift it off, 3 times. 3. Do the same with strip C 8 times, and strip D 15 times. 4. Use a new part of the cloth each time.
flow.say: Look at the sticky side after dabbing. Can you see tiny threads stuck on it? Each dab covers a bit more of the glue.
flow.kid: Leave strip A alone. Press strip B on the cloth and lift it. Do it 3 times. Do strip C 8 times. Do strip D 15 times. Look at the sticky side. What do you see?

ask.q: What is stuck on the tape after dabbing?

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table in a notebook. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason for each strip, and write the guesses beside the table.
flow.say: Which strip do you think will hold a note best? Which one will come off without tearing the paper? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw the table. Guess which strip holds a note best. Guess which one won't tear the paper. Say why.
flow.parent: Wait for a reason as well as a guess. A common guess is 'A is best at everything, because it is the stickiest.' Don't correct it. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the newspaper flat. 2. Use each strip to tape one paper note across its top edge onto the newspaper. 3. Rub each strip once with your thumb. 4. Lift the newspaper by one corner and shake it gently 3 times.
flow.say: Every strip gets one thumb rub and the same three shakes. That keeps the test fair. Which notes stayed on?
flow.kid: Tape one note onto the newspaper with each strip. Rub each strip once with your thumb. Lift the page by a corner. Shake it gently 3 times. Which notes stayed on?
flow.parent: Strip A will almost always hold. Strip D often falls off. Write yes or no for each one in the table.

flow.do: 1. Lay the page flat again. 2. Peel each strip off slowly, one at a time. 3. Look at the newspaper under each one. 4. Write yes, a little, or no for tearing.
flow.say: Peel slowly. Now look at the paper where the tape was. Is there a grey furry patch? That means some paper came away with the tape.
flow.kid: Peel each strip off slowly. Look at the paper under it. Is there a furry torn patch? Write yes, a little, or no.
flow.parent: Fresh tape on newspaper usually lifts a grey, furry patch or tears a strip. The dabbed strips usually peel off clean. If even strip A comes off clean, press it down again, rub it hard with a fingernail, wait 5 minutes and peel again.

check.q: Fresh tape tore the newspaper when you peeled it. Why?
options: The glue gripped the paper's fibres harder than the fibres gripped each other
check.why: Paper is a mat of tiny fibres. Fresh glue holds the top fibres so tightly that they come away with the tape. Picking 'too weak' gets it the wrong way round: the tape was too strong for the paper. Wet paper tears easily too, but the newspaper here was dry.

flow.do: 1. Take each strip that still has some stick, with its note. 2. Stick it on a fresh part of the newspaper, rub once, and shake. 3. Peel and stick it again, up to 5 times. 4. Count how many times it still held.
flow.say: A good sticky note can be moved again and again. Let's count how many times each strip sticks again and still holds its note.
flow.kid: Stick each strip again in a new place. Rub once. Shake. Did it hold? Peel it and try again. Count up to 5.
flow.parent: Strip A often sticks again poorly, because torn paper fibres now cover its glue. A lightly dabbed strip, often B or C, may stick again several times. Results differ with the cloth and the tape, and that is fine. What matters is what your child saw.

flow.do: Ask your child to read the table and say which strip is best for each job.
flow.say: Which strip would you use to hold a poster up for a month? Which one for a note you want to move around a book? Was A the best at everything?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which strip is best for a poster that must not fall? Which is best for a note you can move? Was A best at everything?

ask.q: Was the strongest tape best at every job?
good: No. It held best, but it tore the paper.
The weak tape was better for moving a note around.

flow.think: Spencer Silver's weak glue failed as aeroplane glue. Which job was it good at?

experiments.title: Hot or Cold: Which Freezes First?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test the surprising result of Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy in Tanzania in 1963. He found that his hot ice cream mixture froze before cooler ones. Scientists still argue about it.
experiments.question: If we put hot water and cold water in the freezer at the same time, which one starts to freeze first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the hot water or the cold water get ice on top first? Or will they freeze at the same time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two cups that are exactly the same, with the same amount of water, put in the same freezer at the same moment, side by side on the same shelf. Only the starting warmth of the water is different. Check both at the same times.
results_table: Time after going in the freezer
Hot water cup: what do you see?
Cold water cup: what do you see?

materials.item: 2 steel cups or small steel tumblers that are exactly the same
a measuring cup, or a small katori to measure the same amount of water
hot water from a kettle or a flask, not boiling, and cold water from the tap or a pot
a freezer with space for two cups side by side
a phone or clock with a timer, and a notebook

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and carries the hot cup. Use water that is hot but not boiling. Close the freezer quickly each time, so the food inside stays frozen.

schedule.what: Fill two cups, one hot and one cold, put them in the freezer, then check every 15 minutes until one has ice on top. Play a game or read cards between checks.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each check. Write which cup got a skin of ice first, and how many minutes it took.

setup.art: Two identical steel tumblers on a counter, one with steam rising from it and one without, and a measuring cup beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the same amount of hot and cold water into two cups.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands placing the two tumblers side by side on the same freezer shelf.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up puts both cups in the freezer side by side.

setup.art: A child peering into a freezer at the two tumblers, one with a thin white skin of ice on top.
setup.caption: 3. Check every 15 minutes. Which one has ice first?

flow.do: Tell the story of Erasto Mpemba in a few sentences.
flow.say: In 1963, a schoolboy in Tanzania named Erasto Mpemba made ice cream. He put his mixture in the freezer while it was still hot. It froze before his friends' cooler ones. His teacher said he must be confused. What do you think?
flow.kid: In 1963, Erasto Mpemba made ice cream at school in Tanzania. His mixture was still hot. It froze before his friends' cool ones. His teacher said he was confused. What do you think?
flow.context: This is the start of the hot and cold freezing test. You hear about a surprising result that a schoolboy found.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Which cup will get ice on top first, the hot one or the cold one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw the table. Guess which cup gets ice first. Hot or cold? Say why.
flow.parent: Most children guess the cold one, because it has less cooling to do. That is a good reason. Write the guess down.

flow.do: 1. Measure 100 ml of hot water into one cup. 2. Measure 100 ml of cold water into the other. 3. Put both cups on the same freezer shelf, side by side, at the same moment. 4. Start the timer.
flow.say: Same cups, same amount, same shelf, same moment. The only difference is how warm the water is at the start.
flow.kid: The grown-up pours hot water into one cup. You pour cold water into the other. Same amount in both. Put them in the freezer together. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Pour the hot water yourself. Use water that is hot to touch but not boiling, from a flask or a kettle left for a few minutes. Don't put a hot cup on a glass shelf or straight onto frozen food packets. Stand both cups on the same kind of surface.

flow.do: 1. Every 15 minutes, open the freezer, look at both cups, and close it quickly. 2. Write what you see. 3. Between checks, play the card game or read the explanation cards.
flow.say: Look at the top of each cup. Is there a thin white skin of ice yet? Close the door quickly, so the freezer stays cold.
flow.kid: Every 15 minutes, look at both cups. Is there a skin of ice on top? Close the door fast. Write what you see.
flow.wait: Check every 15 minutes. It usually takes 1 to 2 hours for a skin of ice to form.
flow.parent: In most home freezers, the cold water gets ice first. Sometimes the hot one does. If both freeze at about the same check, write 'same time'. A skin of ice is the easiest thing to judge. Don't wait for the whole cup to turn solid.

flow.do: Read the table together and compare the result with the guess.
flow.say: Which one got ice first? Was your guess right? Mpemba's result was real for his ice cream. Why do you think many tests since then got a different answer?
flow.kid: Which cup got ice first? Was your guess right? Many scientists got a different answer from Mpemba. Why might that be?

ask.q: Why might different people get different answers in this test?
good: The hot water loses some water as steam.
It is hard to decide exactly when water has frozen.

check.q: Mpemba's teacher said he was confused. What was the best thing to do about his result?
options: Forget it, because a teacher said so
Test it again, fairly, and see
Believe it, because he saw it once
check.why: One result can be a fluke, and a teacher can be wrong. The way to find out is a fair test, repeated. Denis Osborne did that, and saw the effect too. Picking 'believe it' trusts one try. Picking 'forget it' trusts a person instead of a test.

flow.do: Repeat the test another day, if your child wants, swapping which side of the shelf each cup goes on.
flow.say: Scientists repeat a test before they trust it. If we try again with the cups swapped, will we get the same answer?
flow.kid: Scientists always test again. Shall we try again another day? This time swap the cups' places.
flow.think: If your answer was different from Mpemba's, does that mean he was wrong? Or that his freezer and cups were different?

activities.title: Who Made the Panakam?
activities.context: In this activity the family makes panakam, a jaggery drink from South India, and each person does one job. Then you decide who should get the credit.

materials.item: jaggery, about 4 tablespoons, grated or broken small
2 tumblers of water
1 lemon, a pinch of dry ginger powder and 2 crushed cardamom pods
a jug, a spoon and a tea strainer
paper slips and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the lemon. Wash hands before making food.

schedule.what: Make panakam together, each person doing one job. Then write a one-line news report and decide who it should name.

activities.record: Write the news report, then write a fair credit list for the panakam.

setup.art: A family around a kitchen counter with a jug, a heap of grated jaggery, a lemon and small bowls of spices, each person holding a different thing.
setup.caption: 1. Give each person one job in making panakam.

setup.art: A girl writing on a paper slip headed 'News', with a jug of brown panakam and tumblers beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Write a one-line news report. Whose name goes in it?

flow.do: 1. Give out five jobs. 2. One person measures the jaggery and one stirs it into the water. 3. One squeezes the lemon, one adds the spices, and one strains and serves.
flow.say: We are going to make panakam together. Each of us has one job. Nobody can make it alone today.
flow.kid: Today the family makes panakam together. Everyone gets one job. What is your job?
flow.context: This is the start of the panakam activity. Each person does one part of the work.

flow.do: 1. Stir the jaggery into the water until it dissolves. 2. Add the lemon juice, ginger and cardamom. 3. Strain it into tumblers.
flow.say: Taste it. Is it good? Now, which job mattered most?
flow.kid: Stir in the jaggery until it disappears. Add lemon, ginger and cardamom. Strain it. Taste it!
flow.parent: Cut the lemon yourself. If only two of you are at home, each person does two or three jobs.

flow.do: Ask your child to write a one-line news report about the panakam, with room for only one name.
flow.say: Imagine a newspaper writes one line about our panakam, and it has room for only one name. Whose name should it be? Why?
flow.kid: A newspaper has room for one name only. Whose name goes in the report about the panakam? Why?

ask.q: Is it fair to name only one person?

flow.do: Now write a credit list, like the end of a film, naming every job and who did it.
flow.say: The pulsar paper had five names on it, but the Nobel Prize named only her supervisor. A credit list names everyone. Let's make one for our panakam.
flow.kid: Make a credit list. Write each job and who did it. Everyone gets a line.
flow.think: Which job did nobody notice, until you wrote the list?

activities.title: Find the Scruff
activities.context: In this activity you search a long paper chart full of random wiggles for one small, regular pattern, the way Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first pulsar.

materials.item: a long strip of paper about 1 metre long: newspaper strips taped end to end, or the back of an old calendar cut into strips
a pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: A grown-up draws a wiggly chart with a hidden pattern. The child hunts for it, then checks it repeats.

activities.record: Circle the pattern each time you find it. Measure the gap between them with a ruler.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand drawing a long, messy wiggly pencil line along a paper strip, with three small identical zigzags hidden in it at equal gaps.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up draws a long wiggly line with a hidden pattern.

setup.art: A child crawling along a paper strip on the floor, circling a small zigzag with a pencil and measuring the gap to the next with a ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Find the pattern. Does it come back at the same gap?

flow.do: 1. Without your child watching, draw a long, messy wiggly line along the whole strip. 2. Hide the same small shape, a sharp double zigzag, at three places exactly 20 cm apart. 3. Make the rest of the line messy, with bigger random bumps too.
flow.say: This is like a radio telescope chart. Somewhere in this mess there is a real signal. Can you find it?
flow.kid: This is like a radio telescope chart. It is full of messy wiggles. One small shape is a real signal. Can you find it?
flow.parent: Make the hidden zigzag small, about 1 cm wide, and make some random bumps bigger than it. The point is that a real signal is not always the biggest mark. It is the one that repeats.
flow.context: This is the start of Find the Scruff. A grown-up draws a messy chart with a small pattern hidden in it.

flow.do: Let your child search the strip and circle anything that looks unusual.
flow.say: Circle anything that looks odd. Is any shape the same each time? Measure the gaps with the ruler.
flow.kid: Look along the whole chart slowly. Circle anything odd. Is one shape the same each time? Measure the gaps between them.
flow.parent: Your child may circle big random bumps first. Ask: does that one come back? A random bump does not repeat. The hidden zigzag comes back every 20 cm.

flow.do: Talk about what makes a mark a signal and not noise.
flow.say: Bell Burnell's scruff kept coming back from the same part of the sky, at the same time by the stars. That is how she knew it was real. How did you know your pattern was real?
flow.kid: How did you know your shape was the real signal? Bell Burnell's mark came back again and again. That told her it was real.

check.q: Bell Burnell saw a strange mark on her chart. What showed it was a real signal from space?
options: It was the biggest mark on the chart
It came back, keeping time with the stars
check.why: Her mark was small, not big. It came back about four minutes earlier each day, just as the stars rise four minutes earlier each day. Signals from Earth do not do that. Picking 'the biggest mark' is a common idea, but noise can be big. A real signal repeats in a pattern.

activities.title: Ask a Grown-up: a Happy Accident
activities.context: In this activity you interview a grown-up about a time a mistake or an accident turned out well. Families have their own small discoveries.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil, or a phone to record the answers

schedule.what: Interview a grandparent, parent or neighbour about a happy accident, then draw it as a comic strip.

activities.record: Write down the answers, then draw the story in four boxes: the plan, the accident, the surprise, and what happened next.

setup.art: A girl sitting with her grandmother on a sofa, holding a notebook, the grandmother laughing as she tells a story.
setup.caption: 1. Ask a grown-up about a mistake that turned out well.

setup.art: A comic strip of four boxes drawn by a child: a pot on a stove, a spill, a surprised face and a happy family eating.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the story in four boxes.

flow.do: Help your child ask these questions: What were you trying to do? What went wrong? What surprised you? Did you ever do it that way again on purpose?
flow.say: Scientists are not the only ones who find things by accident. Let's ask Paati about a mistake that turned out well.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up these questions. What were you trying to do? What went wrong? What surprised you? Did you do it again on purpose?
flow.parent: Kitchen stories work well: a batter left out too long, a dish with a wrong spice that the family now loves, a plant that grew from a thrown-away seed.
flow.context: This is the start of the happy accident interview. You ask a grown-up about a mistake that turned out well.

flow.do: Draw the story in four boxes: the plan, the accident, the surprise, what happened next.
flow.say: Did they check it again, by doing it on purpose? That is the step that turns a lucky accident into something you know.
flow.kid: Draw four boxes. The plan. The accident. The surprise. What happened next.

ask.q: What turned the accident into something the family knows?
good: They did it again on purpose.

activities.title: The Penicillin Credit Roll

materials.item: a long strip of paper, about 50 cm, and two pencils or sticks to roll it on
colour pencils

schedule.what: Write the penicillin team's names and jobs on a paper strip and roll it like film credits.

flow.kid: Write each name and their job on the strip. Fleming noticed the mould. Florey led the team. Chain made it pure. Heatley made enough of it. Hodgkin found its shape.

projects.title: My Surprise Notebook
projects.context: In this 5-day project you keep a notebook of surprises: small things each day that did not happen the way you expected. On the last day you test one of them.

materials.item: a small notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Write and watch only. Don't touch or taste anything strange you find, such as mould or an unknown plant. Show a grown-up instead.

schedule.what: Set up the notebook with columns: date, what I expected, what happened, my guess why.
Write down at least one surprise from the day.
Write down at least one surprise. Read back the first ones. Do any look alike?
Write down one more surprise. Choose the one you most want to explain.
Test your chosen surprise again on purpose. Did it happen again?

projects.record: Five days of notebook entries, and a short note on day 5 saying whether your surprise happened again when you tried it on purpose.

setup.art: A notebook page ruled into four columns headed Date, I expected, What happened, My guess why, with one row filled in.

setup.art: A child at a kitchen window writing in a notebook while looking at a crow on the ledge.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, write down one thing that surprised you.

setup.caption: 3. On day 5, test one surprise again on purpose.

flow.do: Help your child rule four columns: Date, I expected, What happened, My guess why. Fill in one example together.
flow.say: Scientists keep notebooks so that small surprises don't get forgotten. Bell Burnell's scruff was found because she wrote everything down. Let's make yours.
flow.kid: Rule four columns. Date. I expected. What happened. My guess why. Write one surprise from today.
flow.parent: A good first example: 'I expected the ice in my water to sink. It floated.' Any small surprise counts.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Surprise Notebook. You set up a notebook to catch small surprises, the way scientists do.

flow.do: At the end of the day, ask for one surprise and help write it down.
flow.say: What happened today that you didn't expect? Even a small thing counts.
flow.kid: What surprised you today? Write it in your notebook. Small things count.

flow.do: On day 4, read back all the entries together and choose one to test.
flow.say: Which surprise do you most want to explain? Can we make it happen again on purpose?
flow.kid: Read all your surprises. Which one do you want to explain? Can you make it happen again?

flow.do: On day 5, try to make the chosen surprise happen again on purpose. Write down whether it did.
flow.say: If it happens again when we try on purpose, it was not just luck. That is how an accident starts to become a discovery.
flow.kid: Try to make your surprise happen again. Did it happen? Write it down. Was it luck or a pattern?

ask.q: Your surprise happened again on purpose. What does that tell you?

challenges.title: The Bookmark That Stays

challenges.problem: Design a bookmark that stays exactly on the right page when the book is turned upside down and shaken, and comes out without tearing or marking the page.
constraints: The book must be shaken gently three times, upside down, and the bookmark must stay.
When you take it out, the page must have no tear and no mark.

an old book or notebook to test with
general: A paper clip slid over the top of the page holds by squeezing, with no glue at all.
A corner bookmark: a small paper pocket that fits over the corner of the page.
A ribbon or thread fixed to the book's spine, like in many thick books.
Tape dabbed on a cloth until it holds lightly, like Silver's weak glue.
creative: A magnet bookmark: two small magnets in a folded card that clip onto the page from both sides.
A long strip of card folded in a V that grips the page by springing back.
A rubber band around the whole book, holding a plain slip of paper in place.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own bookmark. Draw it, make it, and test it with three upside-down shakes. Then check the page for tears and marks.

flow.do: Put a plain paper bookmark in a book, turn it upside down and shake it.
flow.say: In 1974, Art Fry sang in a church choir. His paper bookmarks kept falling out of his song book. He wanted one that would stay but not tear the pages.
flow.kid: Put a plain bookmark in a book. Turn the book upside down. Shake it. What happens?
flow.context: This is the start of The Bookmark That Stays. You see the problem Art Fry had with his song book.

flow.kid: Draw two bookmark ideas. Which one will stay but not tear the page? Make your best one.

flow.kid: Shake the book three times. Did it stay? Take it out. Is the page clean? What will you change?

good: It holds lightly and lets go cleanly.

challenges.title: A Fair Credit Wall
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about credit. Design a way to thank everyone who worked on a big project, so that nobody is left out.
challenges.problem: Your building is putting up a poster about the people who cleaned up the terrace garden. Thirty people helped in different ways. Design a poster that gives everyone fair credit, but is still easy to read.
constraints: It must fit on one A4 sheet.
Every one of the 30 people must be included.
A visitor must be able to see in 10 seconds what kinds of work were done.
general: List everyone in alphabetical order, so no name seems more important.
Group names by the job they did, like film credits.
Put a group photo with a small name label on each person.
creative: Draw a tree, with each job as a branch and each person as a leaf.
Write the names in a spiral, with no first or last name.
Make each name the same size, and show how many hours each job took with little clocks.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own fair credit poster. When it is done, ask someone to look at it for 10 seconds. Can they say what jobs were done?

flow.kid: Thirty people cleaned the terrace garden. They did different jobs. List the jobs. How can one poster thank them all?

flow.kid: Design your poster. Make up 30 names. Check: does any name look more important? Can you see the jobs fast?
flow.parent: A good poster shows the jobs clearly and treats names equally. Some children decide the planner should be bigger. That is a real choice scientists argue about, so ask for a reason.

flow.say: Did they see the jobs in 10 seconds? The pulsar paper had five names. Bell Burnell was second. What would a fair credit look like for the pulsar?
flow.kid: Show your poster to someone for 10 seconds. Ask what jobs they saw. Did it work?
flow.think: Is it ever fair to give one person more credit than the others?
