opts: Something new that a person builds
Finding out something true that was already there, and showing others
quiz.why: A discovery finds something that was already true, like pulsars. Something new that people build is an invention.

quiz.p: Which of these is an invention, not a discovery?
quiz.why: People made the sticky note. Pulsars, the mould's power and the Raman effect were there before anyone found them.

quiz.p: William Perkin, aged 18, tried to make a medicine for malaria in 1856. What did he make instead?
quiz.why: Perkin's mistake made the first dye from chemicals, a bright purple called mauve. It became hugely popular for clothes.

quiz.p: Fleming saw a clear ring around a mould on his dish of bacteria. What did he do that made it a discovery?
opts: He grew the mould again and tested the result again
quiz.why: He checked. He grew the mould in fresh dishes and saw the bacteria die again. Without the check, it was only a lucky accident.

quiz.p: Why do scientists repeat a surprising result before believing it?
opts: Because most surprising results turn out to be errors or flukes
Because they enjoy doing things twice
Because a prize needs two results
Because the first result is always wrong
quiz.why: A strange result might come from a fault, a mistake or plain chance. If it happens again in a fair test, it is much more likely to be real.

quiz.p: In the Too-Weak Tape Test, which strip is usually best for a note you want to stick and move again?
opts: A strip dabbed on cloth a few times
quiz.why: Fresh tape tears the paper. Tape dabbed many times cannot hold. A strip dabbed a few times holds lightly and comes off clean.

quiz.p: Why did the fresh tape tear the newspaper?
opts: The glue gripped the paper fibres harder than the fibres gripped each other
quiz.why: Paper is a mat of fibres. Strong glue holds the top fibres so tightly that they pull away from the rest of the paper.

quiz.p: Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first pulsar in 1967. Who won the Nobel Prize for it in 1974?
opts: Her supervisor Antony Hewish, with Martin Ryle
quiz.why: The prize went to Hewish and Ryle. Bell Burnell was left out, and people still argue about whether that was fair.

quiz.p: K. S. Krishnan, from Tamil Nadu, did the experiments on light with C. V. Raman. Why is his name less known?
opts: He did not really do any work
The discovery was named after Raman, and only Raman won the Nobel Prize
quiz.why: Krishnan wrote the 1928 paper with Raman. But names on discoveries and prizes give more credit to some people than others.

quiz.p: Which of these is a common reason why people get left out of credit?
opts: They were students, assistants or women at a time when these were taken less seriously
They did not want to be named
quiz.why: Many left-out scientists were young, junior or women. Rules such as the three-person limit on prizes add to the problem.

quiz.p: Divya says, 'Arjun found it by accident, so he gets no credit.' What is the best answer back?
opts: She is right, accidents don't count
Without Arjun's accident there would be no surprise to check, so he deserves some credit
quiz.why: An accident is often the start of a discovery. The noticer, the explainer and the checker all did a part.

quiz.p: Rosalind Franklin took the photograph that showed the shape of DNA. Why was she not included in the 1962 Nobel Prize?
opts: She had died in 1958, and the prize is not given after death
quiz.why: Franklin died in 1958. Watson, Crick and Wilkins won in 1962. Her photograph had been shown to Watson without her knowing, and many people think she deserved far more credit.

items.p: Alexander Fleming came back from a holiday in 1928. On a dish of bacteria, a mould had grown, with a clear ring around the mould. What did the clear ring show?
opts: The bacteria near the mould had died
The mould was eating the glass
The light had faded the dish
items.why: Bacteria cover the dish like a cloudy layer. Where they die, the dish looks clear. So the clear ring showed that something from the mould was killing the bacteria. That something was penicillin.

items.p: Kavya says, 'If an experiment gives the wrong result, it is always useless.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A wrong result can be useful for a different job, like Spencer Silver's weak glue, which became the glue on sticky notes. It also tells you what does not work. A strong answer gives an example.

items.p: Finding something good that you were not looking for, by luck and by noticing, is called ____.
items.why: Serendipity comes from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka. The English writer Horace Walpole made up the word in 1754, from a story about three princes of Serendip who kept finding things by chance.

items.p: Match each person to what they found.
pairs: a purple dye, made by mistake
pulsars, stars that pulse like a clock
a weak glue for sticky notes
C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan
light that changes colour slightly as it scatters
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these is a true discovery. Three began with an accident or a mistake: penicillin, mauve and the weak glue.

items.p: Explain the difference between a discovery and an invention. Give one example of each.
items.a: A discovery is finding something true that was already there, like pulsars. An invention is something new that people make, like the sticky note.
items.why: A strong answer says that a discovery was there before anyone knew it, and an invention did not exist until someone made it.

items.p: Sort each of these: is it a discovery or an invention?
items.a: see items
items.why: Pulsars, the mould's power and the Raman effect were all there before anyone knew. The sticky note, the bicycle and the telescope were made by people. A strong answer asks: was it there before anyone found it?

items.p: In the Too-Weak Tape Test, Lakshmi dabs one strip of tape on a cotton cloth 8 times. What happens to the tape?
opts: Tiny cotton fibres cover parts of the glue, so it sticks more gently
items.why: The cloth leaves tiny fibres on the glue. Where a fibre covers the glue, the glue cannot touch the paper. So the strip grips more gently.

items.p: Draw what you saw on the newspaper after you peeled off the fresh tape. Label the torn part.
items.a: A drawing of the newspaper with a grey, furry patch or a torn strip where the fresh tape was, labelled.
items.why: Fresh tape grips the paper's fibres so tightly that the top fibres come away. A strong drawing shows the rough, furry patch clearly.
items.art: A blank rectangle for a newspaper page.

items.p: Three of these began with an accident or a mistake. Which one began with a careful plan?
opts: James Lind's test of six cures for scurvy
items.why: James Lind planned his test in 1747. He gave six pairs of sick sailors six different treatments to compare them. The other three began with something nobody wanted or planned.

items.p: Jocelyn Bell Burnell found a strange mark on her telescope chart. What did she and her team do first?
opts: Checked whether it was a fault or a signal from Earth
items.why: Most strange results turn out to be errors. So the first job is to check. The team found the mark kept time with the stars, so it came from space, not from Earth.

items.p: Mould had probably landed on other scientists' dishes before 1928. Why do you think Fleming was the one who made it a discovery?
items.a: Fleming had studied substances that kill bacteria for years, so he knew a clear ring was important. He did not throw the dish away. He grew the mould again to check.
items.why: A strong answer mentions that he knew enough to see it was strange, and that he checked it. Louis Pasteur said that chance favours the prepared mind.

items.p: A Nobel Prize can be shared by as many people as did the work.
items.why: False. A Nobel Prize can be shared by at most three people. That is one reason why many people who worked on a discovery are left out.

items.p: Writing or saying who did a piece of work, so that people know and thank them, is called giving ____.
items.why: Credit can be a name on a paper, a name on a discovery, or a prize.

items.p: Divya and her brother Arjun found that curd sets best on top of the fridge. Arjun put his bowl there by accident. Their helper Selvi akka explained why it worked. Divya tested it again to check.

views.says: I found it, so I should get the credit.
It was an accident. I checked it, so it is my discovery.
My mother knew curd likes warmth long ago. I only told you why.

items.ask: Who do you think should get the most credit? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one person with a reason, for example that Divya's check made it sure. It also gives the others their due: without Arjun's accident there was no surprise, and without Selvi akka there was no explanation.
items.why: Real discoveries often need a surprise, an explanation and a check, and different people may do each one. There is no single right answer. What matters is the reason.

items.p: Put the penicillin story in the right order.
items: The Oxford team tests penicillin on mice
Factories make penicillin in huge amounts
Fleming grows the mould again to check
a: Fleming grows the mould again to check
The Oxford team tests penicillin on mice
Factories make penicillin in huge amounts
items.why: First the accident in 1928, then Fleming's check, then the Oxford mouse test in 1940, then mass production during the 1940s. A strong answer sees that the accident was only the first step.

items.p: In 1940, the Oxford team gave eight mice a deadly infection. Four also got penicillin. Why did they give the other four none?
opts: To compare: if only the treated mice lived, penicillin made the difference
items.why: The untreated mice are the control. All eight had the same infection. Only penicillin was different. So when the treated mice lived and the others died, the team knew penicillin was the cause.

items.p: Bell Burnell's strange signal came back about four minutes earlier each day, just like the stars. Explain why this told her the signal came from space.
items.a: The stars rise about four minutes earlier each day, because of how the Earth moves. Signals from cars or radios on Earth keep to our clocks, not to the stars. So a signal that keeps time with the stars must come from out among the stars.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two kinds of timing: Earth signals follow our clocks, star signals follow the stars.

items.p: In 1974, the Nobel Prize for discovering pulsars went to Antony Hewish, who led the project, and Martin Ryle. Jocelyn Bell Burnell, the research student who noticed the signal, was left out.

views.says: She found it. The prize should have included her.
Hewish designed the project and the telescope. Without him there would be no chart to look at.
The supervisor is responsible for a project. Prizes should not usually go to students.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Use what you know about the story. Then answer back from one of the other views.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and backs it with facts, for example that she noticed and checked the signal, or that Hewish built and led the project. It then argues fairly from another side.
items.why: This is a real argument that has gone on for fifty years. Each view has some truth in it.

items.p: Sort each person into the job they did on penicillin.
items.a: see items
items.why: Fleming noticed the mould's effect in 1928. Florey, Chain and Heatley led the Oxford work that made it a medicine. Hodgkin used X-rays to find its shape in 1945.

items.p: Farhan's tape test result: the fresh strip held its note but tore the newspaper. The strip dabbed 15 times fell off at once. The strip dabbed 3 times held and peeled off clean. Which strip is best for a note he wants to move around a book?
items.why: A moveable note must hold, and must come off without tearing. Only the strip dabbed 3 times did both. The fresh one tore the paper and the 15-dab one could not hold.

items.p: Fresh tape is stickier than dabbed tape. So why did the fresh tape do worse when Farhan tried to stick it again after peeling?
items.a: When the fresh tape tore the paper, paper fibres stuck to its glue. The fibres covered the glue, like the cloth fibres did, so it could not grip well the second time.
items.why: A strong answer spots that the torn paper did the same job as the cloth: it covered the glue.

items.p: Louis Pasteur said, 'In the fields of observation, chance favours only the prepared ____.'
items.why: Pasteur said this in 1854. He meant that luck helps people who already know enough to notice that something is strange.

items.p: K. S. Krishnan wrote the 1928 paper about the Raman effect together with C. V. Raman, but only Raman won the Nobel Prize.
items.why: True. Raman and Krishnan did the work together in Kolkata and wrote the paper together. The 1930 Nobel Prize went to Raman alone.

items.p: Label the drawing of tape on paper, seen very close up. Use these labels: paper fibres, glue, tape, cotton fibre covering the glue.
items.a: From top to bottom: tape, glue, paper fibres. A small cotton fibre lies between the glue and the paper in one place.
items.why: A strong answer shows that the cotton fibre stops the glue touching the paper there, which is why dabbed tape grips more gently.
items.art: A close-up side view of a strip of tape pressed on paper, with blank label lines pointing to the layers and to one small thread between the glue and the paper.

items.p: Three of these people were left out of a Nobel Prize for a discovery they worked on. Which one won it?
items.why: Howard Florey shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming and Chain. Heatley, Bell Burnell and Franklin did key work but were not included.

items.p: Meenakshi's grandmother says her mistake, leaving dosa batter out on a hot day, gave the softest dosas ever. What should Meenakshi do to find out if it was more than luck?
opts: Believe it, because Paati is always right
Leave batter out on a warm day again, on purpose, and compare it with batter kept cool
Forget it, because it was a mistake
Ask a friend what they think
items.why: A surprise becomes knowledge only when it happens again on purpose, in a fair comparison. Batter does ferment faster in warmth, so the test would probably work. But testing is how you know.

items.p: Draw a comic strip in three boxes about Henri Becquerel in 1896: the cloudy sky, the drawer, and the fogged plate.
items.a: Box 1: grey clouds and Becquerel waiting with uranium salts. Box 2: the salts in a drawer on top of a wrapped plate. Box 3: the developed plate with a dark shape on it.
items.why: A strong comic shows that the plate fogged in the dark, with no sunlight, which is what showed the uranium was giving out rays by itself.
items.art: Three empty comic boxes in a row.

items.p: Erasto Mpemba's teacher told him he was confused. Was the teacher right to say that? What should the teacher have done instead?
items.a: The teacher should not have decided without testing. He could have put hot and cold mixtures in the freezer and watched. Mpemba's result might have been wrong, but only a test could show it.
items.why: A strong answer says that both a student and a teacher can be wrong, and that a fair test, repeated, is how to find out.

items.p: Match each part of a discovery to an example from the pulsar story.
pairs: a small mark on the chart
it kept time with the stars
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Most discoveries have these four parts. A strong answer can find the same four in another story, such as penicillin.

items.p: Put Spencer Silver's story in order.
items: Sticky notes go on sale in the USA
Silver tries to make a strong glue and makes a weak one
Art Fry needs a bookmark that won't fall out
Silver tells people at his company about his weak glue
a: Silver tries to make a strong glue and makes a weak one
Silver tells people at his company about his weak glue
Art Fry needs a bookmark that won't fall out
Sticky notes go on sale in the USA
items.why: Silver made the glue in 1968 and spent years telling others about it. Fry used it for bookmarks in 1974. Sticky notes went on sale across the USA in 1980.

items.p: Your tape that was dabbed 3 times was a failure as poster tape and a success as note tape. Think of one more 'failure' from your own home that is perfect for a different job. Explain.
items.a: For example, sour curd that is too sour to eat plain is perfect for making mor kuzhambu or soft dosa batter.
items.why: A strong answer names the failure, the job it failed at, and the new job it is good for, and says why. It shows that 'failure' depends on the job.

items.p: A school in Madurai wants to name its new science room after one scientist from Tamil Nadu. Two names are suggested: C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan.

views.says: Name it after Raman. He won the Nobel Prize, and children everywhere know his name.
Name it after Krishnan. He did the experiments too, and almost nobody knows his name.

items.ask: Which name would you choose? Give your reasons. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer chooses one with a reason, such as fame that inspires children, or fairness to a forgotten scientist. It also gives the other side its due, and may suggest a third way, like naming it after both.
items.why: This is a real kind of choice about credit. Both reasons are good ones.

items.p: Science papers today can have hundreds of authors. The 2016 paper on gravitational waves had more than a thousand. What problem does this make for prizes that name at most three people?
opts: No problem, because only three people really did the work
It is hard to choose three people fairly from a huge team
Papers with many names are wrong
items.why: When a thousand people build the machine, run it and check the results, picking three for a prize leaves almost everyone out. People are arguing about whether prizes should change.

items.p: The popular story of penicillin names only Alexander Fleming. Write a fairer version of the story in four sentences.
items.a: In 1928, Fleming noticed that mould killed bacteria on his dish. In 1940, Florey, Chain, Heatley and their Oxford team made it pure and showed it cured infected mice. Factory teams in Britain and the USA learned to make it in huge amounts. Dorothy Hodgkin found its shape in 1945.
items.why: A strong answer includes the noticing, the making, the testing and the many people, and keeps it short and true.

items.p: Most surprising results in science turn out to be real discoveries.
items.why: False. Most surprising results turn out to be errors: a fault in a machine, a mistake in measuring, or a fluke. That is why scientists check and repeat before they believe them.

items.p: Bell Burnell's first idea, half as a joke, was that the signal might come from aliens. Then she found a second pulsing signal in a different part of the sky. Why did that make aliens unlikely?
opts: Two sets of aliens far apart signalling in the same strange way at the same time was very unlikely
items.why: One signal could be anything. Two, far apart, behaving the same way, pointed to a natural kind of object that exists in many places. That object is a spinning dead star, a pulsar.

items.p: Arjun says, 'If I am the first person ever to see something, then it is my discovery.' Is seeing something first enough? Use an example from this unit.
items.a: Seeing it is not enough. You must also check it, explain it and tell others so they can see it too. Mould had landed on dishes before, but Fleming checked and wrote about it. Bell Burnell's signal was on the chart in August, but it became a discovery only when she noticed it and checked it.
items.why: A strong answer says that a discovery needs checking and sharing, and uses a real example.

items.p: Three of these were found while trying to do something else. Which one was found by looking for exactly that?
opts: Mauve dye (Perkin was making a medicine)
The weak glue (Silver wanted a strong one)
The cure for scurvy in Lind's test (Lind was testing cures for scurvy)
items.why: Lind set out to find which cure worked, and found it. The other three found something different from what they were trying to do.

items.p: Kavya's freezer test: her hot water got ice after 90 minutes, and her cold water after 60 minutes. Erasto Mpemba found the opposite. What is the best thing to say?
opts: The result may depend on the freezer, the cups and the mixture, so more fair tests are needed
items.why: Different freezers and containers can give different results. Mpemba's was ice cream mixture, not water. Scientists still argue about this, so the honest answer is to test more, carefully.

items.p: Label the parts of a discovery on this timeline of Becquerel's 1896 story: the plan, the accident, the surprise, the check.
items.a: Plan: put uranium salts in sunlight on a wrapped plate. Accident: the sky was cloudy, so he put them in a drawer. Surprise: the plate was fogged anyway. Check: he did it again in the dark and got the same result.
items.why: A strong answer finds each part. The check was the step that showed the uranium itself was giving out rays.

items.p: Norman Heatley found ways to grow and clean enough penicillin for the Oxford tests. His work was finally honoured by Oxford University in the year ____.
items.why: In 1990, 45 years after the Nobel Prize, Oxford gave Heatley an honorary doctorate in medicine, the first given to someone who was not a doctor.

items.p: Spencer Silver spent years telling people about his weak glue before anyone found a use for it. Why do you think he kept going?
items.a: He thought a glue that holds lightly and lets go cleanly was unusual and must be useful for something, even if nobody had found the job yet.
items.why: A strong answer sees that he believed the result was interesting in itself, not only for the job he first wanted.

items.why: Each of these people did key work. Some won other honours later, but they are left out of the famous version of the story.

applications: Antibiotics such as penicillin, found from a 'spoilt' dish, now cure infections that once killed many people.
Low-tack glues, like the one on sticky notes, are used for removable labels, painters' masking tape and medical dressings that come off the skin gently.
Radio astronomers use pulsars as very exact clocks in space, to study gravity and to look for ripples in space called gravitational waves.
Chemical dyes, starting from Perkin's mauve, colour most of the clothes we wear.
The Raman effect is used to find out what a material is made of without touching it, for example to check medicines and gems.
Scientists use credit lists and author rules to decide whose names go on papers. Some journals now ask every author to say what they did.

open_questions.q: How many discoveries are sitting unnoticed in old records?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep finding new things in old photographs of the sky and old notebooks. Nobody knows how much is still hidden there, because nobody has looked at it all.

open_questions.q: What is the fairest way to give credit when a thousand people make one discovery?
open_questions.why_open: Prizes, author lists and named discoveries were set up when teams were small. Scientists are still trying out new ways, such as lists of who did which job.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a pulsar make its radio beam?

maths.problem: Bell Burnell's pulsar sends one pulse every one and a third seconds. That is 3 pulses every 4 seconds. How many pulses arrive in 12 seconds?
maths.explain: 3 pulses come every 4 seconds. 12 seconds is 3 lots of 4 seconds, because 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. So there are 3 lots of 3 pulses. 3 × 3 = 9.
maths.context: This is about the first pulsar, found by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967. It sends radio pulses as regular as a clock.
maths.why_maths: A pulse that comes at a fixed rate lets you predict exactly how many will come. That is how the team knew the signal was regular, not random.

maths.problem: In the Too-Weak Tape Test, Kavya's strips stuck again this many times: fresh strip 1, dabbed 3 times 5, dabbed 8 times 3, dabbed 15 times 0. Which strip stuck again most, and how many more times than the fresh strip?
maths.answer: The strip dabbed 3 times. It stuck again 4 more times than the fresh strip.
maths.explain: The strip dabbed 3 times stuck again 5 times. The fresh strip stuck again 1 time. 5 − 1 = 4. So it stuck 4 more times. The pattern is not 'more dabs, fewer sticks' all the way: the fresh strip did badly because torn paper covered its glue.
maths.context: Remember the Too-Weak Tape Test, where you dabbed tape on cloth and counted how many times it would stick again? These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which strip did best, and shows that the best one is in the middle, not at either end.

maths.problem: Fleming saw the clear ring in 1928. Penicillin was first given to a patient in 1941. How many years did it take to turn the accident into a medicine?
maths.explain: 1941 − 1928 = 13. Count on from 1928: 2 years to 1930, then 11 more to 1941. 2 + 11 = 13.
maths.context: This is about penicillin. Fleming noticed the mould's effect in 1928, and the Oxford team first gave penicillin to a patient in 1941.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting dates shows how long a discovery really takes. The famous moment was quick, but the work took years.

maths.problem: Kavya's freezer test: the cold cup got ice at 60 minutes, and the hot cup at 90 minutes. She checked every 15 minutes. How many checks did she make before the hot cup got ice?
maths.explain: She checked at 15, 30, 45, 60, 75 and 90 minutes. That is 6 checks. Or: 90 ÷ 15 = 6.
maths.context: Remember the hot and cold freezing test, where you checked two cups in the freezer every 15 minutes? These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal steps of time tells you how often to check, and how precise your result is. Kavya only knows the hot cup froze some time between 75 and 90 minutes.

roots.context: We have made tape weaker on purpose and heard true stories of mistakes that became discoveries. Now we ask what a 'mistake' really is, and who a discovery belongs to.

deep_truth.truth: Your fresh tape held best, but it tore the newspaper when you peeled it. The tape you dabbed on cloth held less, and came off clean. Which tape was best depended on the job you gave it. A result is called a mistake only when it misses what someone wanted.
deep_truth.habit: We sort results into successes and failures as if that were part of the result itself. But the same weak glue was a failure for building aeroplanes and a success for sticky notes. The glue stayed the same. Only the question asked of it changed.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Too-Weak Tape Test, strips from one roll were changed only by the number of dabs on a cloth. The fresh strip won at holding and lost at peeling clean. A lightly dabbed strip lost at holding and won at peeling clean and sticking again.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who can notice a surprise and ask why. That is where every discovery starts.
three.what_is_life: Penicillium mould was making penicillin long before any person noticed. Living things had found it first.
three.what_is_this_world: Pulsars spun in space for millions of years before 1967. The world is full of things that are there before anyone finds them.

roots.thread: The tape behaved in one way, whoever was watching. Its glue gripped the paper fibres harder than they gripped each other. That one happening was a failure to someone who wanted a clean page and a success to someone who wanted a firm hold. The many meanings come from the many people asking different questions. The happening underneath stays one and the same.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching says that hard and easy, long and short, high and low make each other. We know one only by comparing it with the other.
teachings.link: Your tape was 'strong' or 'weak' only compared with the job and with the other strips. Success and failure are named the same way, by comparing a result with what someone wanted.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told of a king who asked men who could not see to touch an elephant. Each touched one part, the trunk, an ear, a leg, and each described a different animal. Each was partly right.
teachings.link: A discovery has many parts, like the elephant. The noticer, the checker, the maker and the explainer each held one part. A story that names only one of them describes only one part.

science.text: Many major discoveries, including penicillin, radioactivity and pulsars, began with unexpected results that the people involved recorded at the time.
Large discoveries today are made by big teams. The 2016 paper announcing gravitational waves listed more than a thousand authors.

other_view.view: They say a failed experiment really is a failure: it was built to answer one question and did not answer it. Most failures never turn into anything useful. Calling every mistake a hidden success can make people careless about getting things right.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Too-Weak Tape Test: fresh cello tape on plain newspaper usually lifts a grey, furry patch or tears a strip when peeled, especially after a firm rub. Dabbing on a cotton cloth leaves visible fibres on the glue, and each dab weakens the strip, so 15 dabs usually cannot hold a paper note. Results vary with the tape, the cloth and the paper, so the step says to rub harder and wait 5 minutes if even the fresh strip comes off clean. The test takes about 30 minutes. Hot or cold freezing test: 100 ml of water in a steel tumbler usually gets a skin of ice in 1 to 2 hours in a home freezer, and in most homes the cold cup freezes first. The step says this honestly and treats any result as a real result. Panakam needs only jaggery, water, lemon and spices. Find the Scruff and the credit roll need paper and a pencil. The spine (intro, the Too-Weak Tape Test, Who Made the Panakam?, explanations, roots and quiz) fits about 85 minutes in two sessions.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1967, Jocelyn Bell was a research student at Cambridge University in England. She had helped to build a radio telescope, a field of wooden posts and wires bigger than two football grounds. It recorded radio waves from space as a wiggly ink line on long rolls of paper. Bell checked the paper by hand, many metres every week. Among the wiggles she noticed a small mark that she called 'a bit of scruff'. It kept coming back from the same patch of sky. On 28 November 1967 a faster recording showed what it was: a pulse every one and a third seconds, as regular as a clock. At first the team wondered if it was a fault, or radio noise from people on Earth. But the signal came back four minutes earlier each day, keeping time with the stars. Half as a joke, they named it LGM-1, for 'little green men'. Then, in December, Bell found a second source pulsing in another part of the sky. Two sets of aliens signalling at the same time was very unlikely. The pulses came from spinning dead stars, now called pulsars. The 1974 Nobel Prize went to her supervisor, Antony Hewish, and to Martin Ryle, not to her.
how_we_found_out.who: Jocelyn Bell (now Jocelyn Bell Burnell), a research student, with her supervisor Antony Hewish, at Cambridge University
how_we_found_out.when: August to December 1967 (the signals), February 1968 (the paper in the journal Nature), 1974 (the Nobel Prize)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: At first the team thought the mark might be a fault in the machine or radio noise from Earth, and joked that it might be aliens. The signal kept time with the stars, so it came from space. A second pulsar elsewhere in the sky showed it was something natural, not a message.
